title: Whittled oak peg hook
subtitle: A single-peg coat hook cut from a branch fork
excerpt: A natural-fork coat hook in seasoned oak: the fork angle makes the hook, the main stem is the wall-mount, and the whole thing is cut to shape with a knife and finished with danish oil. A project that uses the wood's natural geometry rather than fighting it.

glossaryTerms.definition: Air-dried or kiln-dried wood at a stable moisture content for indoor use (8 to 12 per cent). Does not shrink after working.
A short straight-bladed knife with a stout handle; the Swedish school-craft standard for whittling and spoon-carving.

content.text: A peg hook from a branch fork uses the angle of the fork as the hook geometry; there is no bending, steam-forming, or gluing. The hook projects at 45 to 60 degrees from the wall-mount stem. A single coat or bag hangs from it. This project works in
seasoned wood
oak because oak is strong enough in thin cross-section and seasons to a stable piece that will not crack on the wall after fitting. Beginner level, knife only.
Before you start cutting.
Grip: four-finger grip on the work; thumb-push grip on the knife. Never make a cut whose blade-path can reach a body part.
Cut direction: push cuts (blade away from body) and thumb-pivot cuts are the default. Pull cuts only with the work braced against the chest and the blade-arc unable to reach anything vital.
Sharpening: a dull tool is more dangerous than a sharp one. The dull tool slips. Strop every fifteen minutes of carving, hone weekly, oilstone monthly.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
Workspace: stable seat, good light, no children or pets within arm-and-blade reach.
Wood

Find a seasoned oak branch fork where the main stem is 3 to 4 cm in diameter and the side branch meets it at 40 to 60 degrees. The side branch becomes the hook: it needs to be at least 8 cm long after the fork. If oak fork pieces are not available, ash, hazel, or hawthorn work equally well. Hazel in particular seasons quickly and the forks are plentiful from coppice offcuts. The piece must be fully
seasoned
: put it in a dry shed for at least three months after cutting, or take it from material that has already been stored.
Tools
Sloyd knife: shaping and bark removal.
Chip carving knife (optional): for any detail or chamfering at the hook tip.
Leather strop: strop regularly; oak is hard.
Danish oil: durable finish for a wall-hung item.
Method
Step 1: Assess the fork

Before cutting, hold the fork against a wall and decide which way it sits flat. The wide flat back of the main stem goes against the wall; the side branch projects forward. Mark the back flat if the stem is round. Mark the length of the wall-mount stem: it needs to be 12 to 15 cm to give enough bearing surface for two screws.
Step 2: Remove the bark
Use the
sloyd knife
to remove the bark in long, thin push cuts along the grain. Oak bark is thin and comes off cleanly. The grain under the bark changes direction at the fork; use short strokes around the fork junction.
Step 3: Flatten the back of the wall-mount

The wall-mount back needs to be flat enough to sit flush. Use a series of push cuts to flatten a 12 cm section of the main stem. You do not need to remove much material: 3 to 5 mm taken off the high points of the round stem is usually sufficient. Check against a straight edge.
Step 4: Shape the hook tip

Trim the side branch to 8 to 10 cm. Round the tip with the sloyd knife. The tip should be blunt and smooth: sharp tips catch fabric. A slight upward cant at the tip helps keep bags and coats on the hook; round the underside of the tip to a dome rather than a flat cut.
Step 5: Drill the mounting holes

Drill two 4 mm pilot holes in the flat back, spaced 10 cm apart on the centreline of the stem. Counter-bore each hole 8 mm deep with a 10 mm bit to recess the screw head. The hook mounts with two 40 mm No. 8 wood screws into a wall plug or a batten.
Finishing

Apply danish oil to all surfaces. Oak takes oil slowly; a second coat after thirty minutes adds depth. Three coats over two days give a hard-wearing finish. Cure for five days before fitting to the wall. Danish oil hardens completely in five to seven days.
Variations
A triple-fork section with three branches becomes a three-peg rack for a hallway.
Leave the bark on the section that faces outward; remove only from the flat back. The bark-on aesthetic suits a rustic or workshop interior.

attrs.cause: The wood was not fully seasoned; it dried further in the heated interior and split along a medullary ray.
attrs.fix: Season oak pieces for at least six months in a dry unheated space before fitting indoors. Do not season in a heated room; the rapid drying causes radial cracking.

attrs.symptom: The knife is not cutting the oak cleanly
attrs.cause: The edge needs honing. Oak is much harder than pine.
attrs.fix: Hone on the oilstone before starting any oak work, not just strop. Oak requires a finer, more polished edge than softwood.
